item.title: Do verifiable metrics overestimate RSI?
item.description:
Last week, METR released their Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic. They estimate that Anthropic “is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025.” They also add that “there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration.” This assessment implies that timelines to ASI could be very short. A naive forecast based on this information says that we will get ASI within a year.

One of the key data points that informed METR’s analysis was a 1.9x increase in the improvement rate of AECI, Anthropic’s internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index. This is particularly notable because METR estimates that the majority of the acceleration, maybe 80%, is from AI contributions, meaning that we could be seeing the start of an RSI loop causing superexponential growth in capabilities, as measured by AECI.

However, an alternative possibility is that Anthropic’s AIs might be assisting with ML research in a way that overfits to AECI such that this acceleration will not be sustained. METR gestures at this when they note that AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks is one of three key uncertainties that could result in them overestimating AI R&D acceleration. In this post, I discuss this uncertainty, why I believe it points to a legitimate reason that AECI improvements may decelerate, and why this deceleration, more than generalization to fuzzy tasks, is the crux of the relationship between verifiable tasks and timelines.

Second-order AECI might be overfit

In order to discuss this topic, it is useful to differentiate between how good a model is at AECI, how good a model is at training models to be good at AECI, how good a model is at training models to be good at training models to be good at AECI, etc. I will use the terms AECI, AECI’, and AECI’’ to refer to each of these properties.

My point rests on the claim that AECI’ can be improved without improving general ML research skills. In theory, “general ML research” is the kind of skill that would keep bearing fruit across any number of AI generations: if gen 1 is better at ML research, then it will be better at making gen 2 better at ML research in a way that makes gen 3 better at ML research, and so on. In contrast, an AI that is good at AECI’ might make choices that improve the next generation's AECI score but don’t make the next generation robustly smarter and better at carrying those improvements down the line.

There are a couple of sources of selection that I believe could lead to overfitting to AECI’ such that it comes apart from general ML research skills.

  1. Humans train AIs and select the ones that are good at AECI’. One way this could happen is by Anthropic directly training against AECI’. For example, they could train AIs on NanoGPT speedrun-type tasks where the AI has to come up with algorithmic improvements to training that increase AIs’ benchmark scores with minimal compute. It’s possible that these algorithmic improvements could be overfit to the benchmarks (these benchmarks could include AECI or be correlated with it) such that they don’t lead to AIs that are more compute efficient across the board. A more subtle way humans might select for AECI’ is by developing a preference for models that seem to be coming up with good ML research ideas but where the quality of the ML research is being measured against (and overfit to) verifiable benchmarks.
  2. AIs train new AIs and select the ones that are good at AECI. Even without humans overfitting to metrics for AECI’, AIs might naturally be more skilled in AECI’ than general ML research. For example, AIs might have poor taste but compensate by iterating harder (compared to humans) against verifiable benchmarks. AIs iterating against W2SG benchmarks (which involve training AIs), for instance, struggled with overfitting. They beat humans on the primary metric, performance gap recovered, but the gain didn’t hold up when transferred to a production-scale setting, and the authors flag finding metrics agents “can reliably hill-climb without overfitting” as a key challenge. In general, AIs may select harder for AIs that score well on benchmarks even if those AIs are less generally intelligent.

These points correspond to the labels 1 and 2 on the diagram below.


Overfitting to AECI’ could be one instance of a broader pattern in which models pick low-hanging fruit, producing a quick speedup that ultimately diminishes. Their jagged intelligence might give them a comparative advantage relative to humans that drives a burst of early insights, but that advantage could dry up as the shared frontier of human and AI insight becomes more saturated. This seems especially likely if AI's comparative advantage rests more on iteration and local improvements than on conceptual taste and systematic improvements.

This early acceleration dynamic is one possible explanation for the jump in the rate of AECI improvement that METR attributes to AI. If this is the case, then ML research improvement from AI could saturate, leading to deceleration later.

Why ML research is the crux

In my analysis, I focus on the gap between AECI’ and general ML research skills in order to separate automated ML improvements that will drive a strong positive feedback loop from those that will eventually level off. However, someone could also be concerned with positive feedback loops on verifiable tasks that don’t translate to positive feedback loops on fuzzy tasks. I put much less credence in this concern because I think we are likely to see at least some transfer between verifiable tasks and fuzzy tasks. This is because some verifiable tasks are central to general improvements in intelligence. Sample efficiency is one example. It can be measured by how few samples an algorithm needs to reach a given score on a benchmark. Sample efficiency is central to intelligence because it gets at generalization: higher sample efficiency means better performance out of distribution. Better out-of-distribution performance, in turn, means better performance on fuzzy tasks, which depend on generalization because directly relevant metrics for them are scarce.

Additionally, the transfer between verifiable tasks and fuzzy tasks does not need to be high. As long as you think that even a small fraction of verifiable capabilities transfer to fuzzy tasks, a FOOM on verifiable tasks will quickly transfer to fuzzy tasks.

Thus, I don’t think there is a compelling case for long timelines on account of AIs struggling to transfer verifiable skills to fuzzy tasks. AI’s acceleration on verifiable tasks will have to saturate in order for timelines to be extended.

Conclusion

The overfitting consideration I have laid out here is only one of many for determining how sustainable the acceleration in AI capabilities will be. For example, it’s possible that there is some degree of overfitting and also an underlying superexponential trend. My all-things-considered view is that there is a 60% chance we will see a deceleration in AI progress in the next two years, but a significant, maybe 30%, chance we will see ASI by the end of 2027.


Thank you to Jadyn Malone, Nabil Baugher, Lukas Finveddan, and Alex Mallen for useful feedback and discussion.

item.title: Characterizing secondary structure representation in ESM-2
item.description:
Methods note: The code used for the experiments and related open-source repo were built with Claude. The experimental design and writeup is my own, with minimal editing and formatting amendments made with Claude

Introduction

This is a research report inspired by a single question: in a model engineered to answer a simple biological question, how are higher-order, auxiliary concepts represented and used? ESM-2 is a model designed to infer missing amino acids in protein sequences (Lin et al. 2023), but what does the model use and know of emergent secondary structure? These are two different questions, and the data in this post serve to distinguish between the two: information about secondary structure is decodable, but when ablated has a limited, quantifiable effect on the model's accuracy. The implications of this research are in service of the greater question: when we use an LLM for a biological task, but we (appropriately) worry about how higher order or secondary concepts are being used by that LLM, how can we monitor or manipulate the representation of those secondary concepts? I personally believe that the bigger questions require parsing the smaller ones first, and so here I characterize the representation and usage of secondary structure (DSSP-labeled helix, strand, or coil) in ESM-2 150M.

Is secondary structure linearly represented?

The experiment to answer this question is relatively simple--use a linear probe to decode the vectors which represent the DSSP-labeled secondary structures, ablate those representations, and compare model performance to ablation of a random plane. The first thing to test is that the ablation worked; how well it worked provides information about the linearity of the concept representation. At layer 29 of 30, performing a linear ablation and then refitting a new linear probe on the same layer decreased decodability (hereafter referenced in macro-F1) from 0.81 to 0.71. This suggests, simply, that while some of the concept is linearly decodable, the linear probe’s plane does not hold all of the relevant signal.

This is not to say that the linearly decodable elements of secondary structure were not predictively significant. Rather, the results were encouraging recapitulations of existing research (Rives et al. 2021; Adams et al. 2025; Gujral et al. 2025) with a meaningful extension of their findings: linear ablation of these concepts reduced true residue likelihood by about 1 percent for helix and strand compared against random vector ablation. This shows that the linear representation of secondary structure is used by ESM-2 , but is not a complete picture of all that is represented by the model about secondary structure.

What, if any, linear direction does the model use for residue prediction?

The linear probe discovered and ablated a plane that removed some, but not all, of the linear decodability of the concept. This tells us that a linear probe alone cannot be used to remove all of the linearly decodable representation. So, how can we ablate all of the linearly decodable information without a linear probe?

The answer comes from removal of the class-mean plane. Each row represented within ESM-2 corresponds to a single amino acid, which we can label as belonging to a class: our secondary structures (helix, strand, coil). For a given cloud of points representing a class, there exists a mean. If we were to superimpose each class cloud over one another such that their means share the same coordinates, no linear plane could be used to distinguish them (Belrose et al. 2023). In this experiment, the refit probe following class mean plane ablation fell to 0.22 (the 0.02 discrepancy coming from the difference between training and test data), proving the ablation to be successful.

Ablation of the class-mean plane decreased true residue likelihood by 6% across secondary structures (Table 1). This suggests that the model uses the linearly decodable differences between secondary structures to infer amino acids based on surrounding residues.

Table 1. Removing one plane at layer 29. Likelihood drop = 1 − exp(Δ), with Δ the mean change in log-likelihood of the true residue at a masked position. Nats in parentheses.

Plane removed New linear probe, macro-F1 Likelihood drop, helix Strand Coil All residues
None 0.81 0 0 0 0
Random plane 0.81 0.1% 0.1% 0.1% 0.1% (−0.001)
Probe's plane 0.71 1.1% 0.9% 0.3% 0.7% (−0.007)
Class-mean plane 0.22 7.1% 4.8% 5.7% 6.0% (−0.062)
Class-mean plane, amino-acid identity held fixed not run 4.9% 2.7% 5.7% 4.8% (−0.049)

This, however, is an incomplete assertion. In order to better understand how the model uses this information, it helps not only to see how the model behaves when the information disappears, but how it behaves when it's given misleading information. In other words, what happens to the model's predictions if you deliberately "mislabel" the secondary structure affiliated with an amino acid? To do this, I added the class-mean vector for helix to rows representing residues labeled with coil. I found that the residue predictions meaningfully shift towards helix-forming amino acids, increasing their predicted probability on coil rows by 13% (Table 2).

Table 2. Adding a direction to coil rows at layer 29. One dose moves the mean of the coil rows onto the helix mean along the direction. Helix-forming amino acids: A, E, F, I, K, L, M, Q, R, W.

Direction added Dose Predicted probability on helix-forming amino acids Share of the helix-coil gap closed Coil rows the layer-29 probe calls helix
None 0 43.6% 0 9%
Helix class-mean direction 0.5 45.9% 0.13 44%
Helix class-mean direction 1 49.2% 0.33 94%
Helix class-mean direction 2 56.3% 0.74 100%
Helix class-mean direction 4 63.1% 1.15 100%
Helix direction, amino-acid identity held fixed 1 48.2% 0.27 94%
Random direction, same length 1 43.4% −0.01 9%

This set of experiments shows that linearly collapsible information about secondary structure is represented and used by ESM-2 for residue prediction, but does not exhaustively represent all information about secondary structure.

What nonlinear representation of secondary structure exists after linear erasure, and how is it used?

Table 3 shows how different non-linear probes decode secondary structure representation following linear erasure and class-means ablation. While most nonlinear probes still decode the information, but are meaningfully affected by the linear erasure, QDA remains unaffected throughout. This suggests that the shape of the class cloud, largely untouched by the ablation, closely mirrors that used by the QDA--a tilted ellipsoid. Of note here is that the squares-only reader, which has an untilted ellipsoid shape, falls from 0.81 to 0.56, suggesting further that the orientation of the ellipsoid is an exceptionally significant element of the concept’s representation within the model.

Table 3. Readers trained after the edit at layer 29. Macro-F1 on held-out chains. Floor 0.20.

Reader Unedited Random plane removed Probe's plane removed Class-mean plane removed
Linear probe 0.81 0.81 0.71 0.22
MLP, one hidden layer 0.81 0.81 0.80 0.79
SVM, RBF kernel 0.82 0.82 0.77 0.78
Squares-only, untilted ellipsoids 0.81 0.81 not run 0.56
QDA, tilted ellipsoids 0.81 0.81 not run 0.81

Perhaps the most interesting finding of this post, ablating the shape of the cloud after class-mean plane erasure decreases true residue likelihood by 2% (Table 4). This suggests that the shape of the data is, itself, used by the model for residue interpolation. Notably, this is only true for helix and strand, but not for coil for which ablation of shape incurs no predictive penalty. This is likely because the shape of coil is affected by its incorporation of a plethora of more disparate secondary structures (“unassigned”), whereas helix and strand are consistent throughout their representative distributions.

Table 4. Removing the shape of the class clouds at layer 29. Last row: paired difference in log-likelihood, shape minus control, converted the same way.

Edit QDA after the edit, macro-F1 Likelihood drop, helix Strand Coil All residues
Class-mean plane alone 0.81 7.1% 4.8% 5.7% 6.0% (−0.062)
Plane plus shape 0.03 11.8% 9.3% 8.2% 9.7% (−0.102)
Control: plane plus shape fit on shuffled labels 0.66 8.4% 6.6% 8.4% 8.0% (−0.084)
Shape beyond the control 3.7% 2.8% −0.2% 1.9% (−0.019 [−0.021, −0.016])

How is this picture shaped by architecture of ESM-2?

ESM-2's bidirectionality within layers (each row reading information from higher and lower rows, representing amino acids flanking it on both sides) affects the difficulty and implementation of concept erasure. As such, the contingency of erasure on identical erasure on surrounding rows as mapped between layers, was performed in Table 5. This meaningfully affects our understanding of the positional distribution of the concept representation: The representation of higher order concepts in ESM-2 is affected by the ability of a row at a given layer to represent bidirectional information about surrounding amino acids and their affiliated secondary structures.

Table 5. Class-mean plane removed at layer 29 at a share of positions. New linear probe trained at layer 30 on the erased rows. Likelihood drop at the same rows.

Positions erased at layer 29 Erased rows read Rows New linear probe at layer 30, macro-F1 Likelihood drop at those rows
None all rows 113,279 0.81 0
Every position all rows 113,279 0.56 6.0%
Half, at random both neighbours also erased 14,069 0.58 4.9%
Half, at random both neighbours intact 14,297 0.66 4.2%
Half, at random three intact on each side 861 0.69 5.3% [3.8%, 6.9%]
One in ten, at random all erased rows 11,508 0.67 3.9%
Half, random plane all erased rows 56,797 0.81 0.1%

To better understand how information about secondary structure is represented across layers, single layer ablations were performed at all layers, and multi-layer ablations were run on band 20-30, 26-30, and 29-30 (Figure 1). The multi-layer ablations prove that secondary structure can be reconstructed across multiple layers, suggesting that ablation at a single layer using these techniques would be insufficient for full concept erasure. The difference in true residue prediction between ablation at Layers 30 and 29 is 8% (14 and 6 respectively), and also suggests meaningful reconstruction happens between single layers, contingent on erasure at proximal positions (Table 5).

Figure 1. Cost of removing the class-mean plane, by depth. A: one layer at a time. B: every layer of a band. C: what a new linear probe reads at layer 30 after each band.

What other experiments would teach us more about secondary structural representation in ESM-2?

The most straightforward experiment assesses its scalability--use the exact experimental paradigm across all ESM-2 sizes (8M, 35M, 150M, 650M, 3B and 15B) and see if increased dimensionality affects the shape and nonlinear properties of the concept representation. Furthermore, assessing the boundary conditions of the conclusions, and amending observations about the model's use of coil shape, would involve increasing the usage of DSSP labels to include all 8, and therefore be more granular.

Methods and Supplementary Data

For fit and test data, 548 chains comprised of 113,279 labeled residues (out of 135,365 total) were used (NetSurfP-3.0 dataset; Hugging Face mirror). 5 folds were grouped by chain, and every score was determined on chains held-out from the training data. The baseline linear decodability of secondary structure is a macro-F1 of 0.81. Guessing always-coil had a macro-F1 of 0.20. Amino-acid alone (without model usage) would provide a macro-F1 of 0.44.

Table 6. Plane removed at every layer of a band. Unedited: top-1 accuracy 39.2%, linear probe 0.81, QDA 0.81.

item.title: What Can AI Welfare Buy Without Consciousness?
item.description:
Lightly edited transcript of a talk given at NYU AI Safety, November 9, 2026. Recording available at https://youtu.be/6WpRfW1d4CM


Joseph Wright of Derby, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons


Introduction

What can we buy while the question of AI consciousness stays open? My answer turns on a distinction between duties to a model and duties with respect to a model. These run through at least two relations, with society and with particular people. I'll try to show that they justify more measures than it seems at first glance, and plausibly more than a low precautionary principle would.


Consider a case. A model keeps failing its tests, and a representation of desperation rises, a representation of calmness falls, and as that happens, the model cheats more and more.


Should we do something about it? There's at least two possible reasons for saying yes. One, the model may be suffering, and second, the states make it less safe. Now note that the first one requires, of course, that the model is a thing that can suffer, and that is the entire question that I'm going to try to set aside. The second needs no such assumption, so I'm going to follow reasons akin to the second here. But let me motivate it a little more.


The first reason sends us to the debate of consciousness, and that's where most of the debate stands. It may be at a stalemate for a while. Skeptics disagree about whether AI systems are or even could be conscious. But both skeptics and advocates agree that consciousness and sentience are the clearest grounds of patienthood. Moreover, people like Seth argue that caring about non-conscious systems would distort the circle of moral concern.


The question may stay open for a long time. Eric Schwitzgebel says, quite bluntly, the experts do not know, you do not know, and all is fog. And his stronger claim is that we will not know before we have built very many systems whose consciousness is disputable.


The disagreement is wide. At one end, Seth defends biological naturalism, saying that consciousness depends on our nature as living organisms. And then on another side of the spectrum, if we can put it that way, Chalmers says that there may be a 25% chance of conscious AI within a decade. I'm not going to choose or debate between them. I'm just going to say, what if it is always an open question? What can we do in the meantime?


There's at least three reasons that this disagreement may not end. First, every confirmed case, every piece of evidence that we have, is biological, which kind of means that biology can do it, biology can give rise to consciousness, but it doesn't discard the possibility of functionalism, that you could have consciousness without biology. The issue is that the evidence that we have does not separate substrate from function. There is some evidence for functionalism and maybe some theoretical advantages. There are some a priori arguments, like the gradual replacement argument, also from Chalmers.


Another issue is that behavior alone cannot break the tie. You have the gaming problem: for any possible behavior, two systems that have the same behavior, one with consciousness and the other one without consciousness, could be indistinguishable if you are just looking at behavior.


If you're into mech interp, you may say, oh, but there's not just behavior. You could look inside. So can interpretability do any better? Well, between substrate views, it cannot adjudicate at all, because substrate views would predict the same mechanisms. They would predict that the mechanisms would look the same for us as we look with mech interp methods. Both for a conscious and a non-conscious system, you would have the same activations, representations. How would we tell whether there's consciousness in there? Mech interp would not say anything. And within functionalism, the indicators are calibrated on human data. And so the reports are the things that we just cannot trust.


There's a further confound, if you're into the introspection literature: something like a desperation vector, maybe the model representing this desperation, either in itself or in a character or on a text. And we yet don't know how to take those apart.


Still, though, interpretability does something that behavior alone doesn't do, or cannot. In Birch's words, the system can't play act with regards to its own architecture. What that means is that mechanistic interpretability can at least show us that a state is causally used, that it has causal power. And that is exactly what my argument is going to use.


So what can we buy in the meantime? I propose that we look for reasons that do not need us to settle our credence in AI consciousness. Our credence may be on a question mark, and the reasons that I'm going to give you are going to apply even though we may just not resolve this.


Two disclaimers. I'm going to take no side on the credences, and I'm going to take no side on whether models are welfare subjects. But I will make one moral claim. I'm going to say that something can matter morally and non-instrumentally without being a welfare subject. That is the type of claims that I'm going to make about models. I'm going to make also welfare claims about people, and you'll see in one of the branches that my argument takes.


Here's the plan. I already gave you a case, and the main question. I'm going to distinguish two kinds of duties, duties to the AI and with respect to it. Duties with respect to the AI run through at least two relations. And then I'm going to ask, for both, what can they buy against the shopping list of what AI welfare advocates may want to buy. And I'm going to contrast also at what cost to safety duties come. And then I'm going to talk briefly about some limits and wrap up.


Two kinds of duties

The distinction is quite old. What matters in duties to is that there is someone who can be wronged. If I fail a duty to X, then X has a complaint. Now, if I fail a duty with respect to X, the complaint belongs to someone else, or to no one in particular.


An example of duties to X: it seems good in itself if animals are able to escape a forest fire without injury, even if nothing further follows. And if I could save an animal from a forest fire and I do not, the animal is wronged, because the animal can suffer. I think it's quite obvious, and I hope I don't need to defend that.


Now, duties with respect to X: you could think of your car's brakes. I have duties with respect to my car's brakes, for the safety of others, for my own safety. Someone else's cars: I have duties to the owners and with respect to their car. With respect to the Grand Canyon, for what it means to people, and how it contributes to their flourishing, as I'm going to argue. And even the internet, that we happen to depend on. I'm going to talk about dependence. There are other examples that we could fit in here, like the ozone layer. It matters for what it does to us, what it allows. And maybe even mountains, that matter as part of our lives.


Back to the animal. Why can the animal be wronged? Well, there are at least two premises. A: duties can be owed only to a being with a good of its own, or, like I put it more colloquially, there are beings that can suffer. And B is that a being has a good of its own only if it's conscious. So duties are owed to the AI only if it's conscious. That's for duties to the AI.


The issue is that this sort of argument inherits all the fog that Schwitzgebel talks about. Moreover, both premises are contested. But even within the consciousness camp, the ground is contested. Consciousness may be necessary without being sufficient. Kagan, for example, imagines a being that is conscious but only ever perceives blue, and it's not obvious that anything could be going better or worse for that being. So many take sentience, the capacity for valenced states, to be the ground, or a more likely ground. Others ask for even more, such as a continuous subject for whom things can be good or bad. I think that's a little strong. But anyways, the idea is that this is very contested. And still, these are the clearest grounds for duties to. And moreover, some people that deny this are those that argue that agency, strong, robust agency without experience, may suffice to make a moral patient or a welfare subject.


Duties with respect to a model don't inherit any of the fog, and they are quite relational. They run through the model's relations to others, and there are at least two. The first one is with society, and it happens that they match up mostly with AI safety, so there's almost no tension, if not any. But maybe not all. Like the internet, some models may be things that society ends up relying on, and then we may have duties with respect to them.


The second relation is with particular people. There may be individual attachment reasons, I'm going to argue, from flourishing and dependence. Neither of these need the models to be conscious, so we shouldn't worry about the fog. In fact, it doesn't apply to us here at all. Prima facie, it seems like duties with respect to don't really support too much. I'm going to try to convince you that they support at least more than it seems. I'm going to take each one in turn, and we'll see if I happen to convince you.


Through society

Let's run through the first argument. I call it the safety argument just because it's so compatible with safety, but maybe I shouldn't call it the safety argument.


  • Premise 1. How we train, describe, and treat models shapes their dispositions.
  • Premise 2. Their dispositions shape their later behavior.
  • Premise 3. The behavior matters for the people it affects.


Therefore, we have reasons with respect to models to treat them in ways that yield good dispositions. And it so happens that some welfare measures are ways of doing so.


Let's go back to the initial case. Some people found that steering toward desperation increases reward hacking, and that the same pair of states, desperation and calmness, drives blackmail. You may have seen the Claude blackmail example from a while ago. So what does this mean? That the internal states are not idle. They're constantly involved in the behavior that safety cares about, which is what my premise two means: that the states and dispositions shape the model behavior, and that it affects people.


One worry is that maybe this only happens under artificial steering, so it's not really a real-life deployed behavior or situation. But that's not really quite the case. Jhaveri et al. show that repeatedly rejecting the model's answers raises its frustration in a natural deployment, and the same sort of reward hacking starts happening. So this happens under ordinary use.


What I want to say is that it may give us a weak duty with respect to the model not to pile rejections onto one thread, and maybe to clear the context when frustration builds up. Of course, it's a defeasible duty, because it depends on what effect, if any, our rejections cause in the model.


Maybe something to note is the unit, or individual, here is the thread, because that's where the states live. The moment you clear the thread, those states are cleared or reset. I'm going to talk more about individuation later.


So the safety argument, or the societal argument through safety, recommends lowering desperation, because it causes cheating, and that may have downstream effects on users. How do we do that? Well, as I said, clear the context, but also maybe let's build environments that do not trigger it to even begin with; maybe steering toward calm, although I'm going to say that that may not be the case; and this may even, possibly, support some sort of monitoring from the inside. But again, keep in mind that the model's own good plays no role here. It's all about its downstream effects.


Now, this argument rejects mood prompting. Mood prompting is the idea that you can prompt the model, system prompt or whatever, and say, you are happy, you are very, very, very happy. The issue is that positive emotion vectors, at least right now, raise sycophancy. And so, because the safety argument picks measures by their effect on behavior, and mood prompting has negative effect on behavior, it rejects mood prompting. So that's already a tension with welfare.


This is quite close to Jhaveri's program. They say that functional welfare should be calibrated, not maximized, just kept within a benign range. They, for example, recommend inducing some lower states in evals through a prior history of failure. But my question is, okay, this just seems like safety. What actual welfare measures are you buying? I hope it becomes clearer as I go.


Functional welfare borrows welfare's indicators. What of welfare does functional welfare actually have if there's no sentience? Well, it borrows at least the indicators. A functional welfare is a set of welfare-like dispositions and states that vary with the representation of how the model is doing relative to its goals. Welfare-like means something like analogous to what indicates high or low welfare in beings with moral status. So we have the indicators and the functional role. But again, it gives no actual welfare reasons of their own. In fact, if more negative states made a model safer, nothing here would object, right? If injecting some sadness into the model made the model way safer, then functional welfare would be okay with it. So, again, maybe we shouldn't call it functional welfare.


Safety is one societal reason among several that I'm going to talk about. Dependence: society may end up relying on a model. Habits: treating a model shapes the one who treats it. And record: a model can matter to history and science. I have to admit that maybe habits should go in the individual relational argument, but that one turns on another requirement, which is being an important component of a user's flourishing, so I decided to keep it here. But know that that one starts touching on individual relations instead of societal relations. Still, that doesn't really undermine any of the arguments.


Dependence. Like the internet, a model is something that whole society, or parts of society, may come to rely on. Different firms and much of our current software may be built around one model and its specific sets of dispositions or behaviors, and retiring it or replacing it may break what was built. That gives some reason to keep it available and/or to warn before it is retired. Again, these reasons concern practices that rely on the model, and they can pull against safety, because the model that some practice relies on may be the model that safety needs to retire, like the GPT-4o situation that we had not too long ago, although in AI it seems like ages ago.


Habits. Kant used to talk about this. He said something like: cruelty to animals corrupts the character of the one who is cruel. The safety argument, the prior argument, applies this idea to the model's character, but this one is to the user's character, and more in its original form. A user who rehearses cruelty on a model may then carry it elsewhere, maybe even more so as we start having humanoids. And that gives a reason to end abusive conversations, and possibly some norms of treatment more broadly. And I think these reasons are quite aligned with safety, especially if these abusive conversations end up in training data that then shape models' dispositions.


Record. A model can matter as part of history and of science, as an archive does. Anthropic actually lists restricting research on past models among the costs of deprecation, and that may give us some reason to preserve weights. It mostly aligns with safety, since studying past models is part of safety research, but it can also pull against safety, since every set of stored weights is a set that can be stolen or misused.


Through particular people

Second argument: through particular people.


  • Premise 1. People form relations with particular models.
  • Premise 2. A model can be part of someone's flourishing, as a landscape can.
  • Premise 3. That flourishing matters.


So we have reasons with respect to models to preserve what those relations need. And it so happens that some welfare measures are ways of doing so.


I take inspiration of this type of argument from Bill FitzPatrick, who makes this sort of argument for landscapes and nature in general, the environment in general. The idea is that some things can have value that is relational and still non-instrumental. In FitzPatrick's words, they are so "as constituent objects of experiences and relationships that are constitutive of human well-being or flourishing." That doesn't mean that the value is intrinsic to the thing. That's not it. But it's also not merely causal either.


A natural objection is that this relation is not real. You may think of an experience machine. If you've taken any phil classes, you might have heard of that. A program makes you feel like you're interacting with humans, but it's not really so. So at most, you have phantom friends. But the experience machine, I think, fails because the relation is not real, because the person, by definition of the experience machine, is cut off from the real world. But a model is a real thing in the world, even if it's electrons and things stored. It's a real thing, and it's physical, right? And talking to it may then create a real relation.


Now, what kind of relation? I leave that open. I think that there are at least two types of relations: like a relation to a landscape, or like a relation to a friend. I'm not going to take a stance on that. It seems to me that a relation that we may establish with the landscape, again, in this constitutive experience, suffices for my claim, which is also the weaker one.


But that doesn't mean that every attachment counts. Again, on FitzPatrick's view, who I'm just stealing from, what gives a thing this value is its constitutive role in a flourishing life, or in well-being. And that role is, in principle, independent of our contingent desires. So this is unlike Korsgaard. Korsgaard would say that our volitions confer value. I reject that. So what's the consequence here? That an attachment that harms the user is not part of their flourishing, so it carries no value of this kind. For example, sycophancy feeds into attachments of that bad kind. So that means attachment reasons have a filter built in, and that's going to matter also when we compare how this fares with respect to tensions with safety.


The test

Let's go to the test. I'm going to take what welfare advocates ask for, and I'm going to ask, one measure at a time, whether each relation supports it or not, and what's the tensions. You're going to see that some measures are widely supported, as I've already been mentioning, and some other in a narrower form, and some others are not supported at all.


The list: I borrowed this from Long and Sebo, Keeling and Street, and Bradley and Saad. There's three groups: measures of knowing, measures of treatment, and rights.


Welfare evals and calibrated self-reports are supported as monitoring. Self-reports are really not enough, because a state can drive behavior and leave no trace in what the model says. So monitoring has to reach inside. And through particular people, there's no reason that I can think of. There's no reason that a user needs to look inside the model.


Ending abusive conversations is supported in a conditional way: if abuse shapes dispositions, then we have support. If abusive conversations shape the persona that the model settles into or drifts into, then we have a safety reason, the first argument. Or if it shapes the habits of the user who is abusing it, then we have a reason from habits. But now, if abuse happened to shape neither, which I don't think is the case, but if that were the case, then I would have no support here. And attachment reasons also give no reason of their own, because abusive relations are not part of anyone's flourishing, so it doesn't even qualify to get into the attachment reasons.


Preserving weights is actually quite supported, and by more than one reason. Anthropic's deprecation commitments list safety risks related to shutdown-avoidant behavior by models among the risks for preservation. Also, record and dependence point in the same way. And through particular people, preserving weights may be what keeps the model that someone relates to in existence.


Here's just a coincidence: Anthropic's four reasons for preserving weights really match up quite nicely. The deprecation commitments, they list four costs of retiring a model: safety risks related to shutdown-avoidant behavior by models, cost to users who value specific models, restricting research on past models, and risks to model welfare. The first one is a safety reason, the second is about attachment and dependence, where the users rely on a model, the third one is a record reason, and only the fourth one is a duty to the model. But note that three of the four need no answer about consciousness.


The original request was: don't make the model suffer. I can support that narrowly, as what I call dispositional hygiene. That means we avoid the states that push the model toward bad behavior, just as we keep training data clean, because of what they cost later. And again, there are two restrictions here that apply. States with no effect on behavior are left alone. And if the stress improved behavior, like I said, the safety model would actually recommend it. Fortunately, in this world, with the current models, that's not the case, but in principle that would be a consequence of my view.


And attachment reasons actually add nothing new here. A person's relation to a model does not need the model to be free of distress, unless they were to harm the user's flourishing that's dependent on their relationship with the model.


Now the rights, the last one in our list. Actually, none of them is supported by my arguments as a right. At most, the safety argument supports some of them in a case-by-case basis when, say, evaluation degrades the model's dispositions. For example, whether deception in evals does so is an open question. Now, through particular people, two of them get some support case by case: not deleting a model when someone's flourishing or well-being depends on it or relates to it, and keeping its persona continuous, again, for the same reason.


Now, six of these welfare measures forbid or conflict with the safety measure, and this is from Long and Sebo. But the tension is conditional on patienthood. And one of these measures changes status with the kind of duty. Internal monitoring is surveillance, or akin to surveillance. On the safety argument, this is required. But if the AI were a patient, it would be wrong. So here I'm trying to make explicit the tensions with safety.


I said that I was going to talk about individuation. What or who are these measures for? Is it the weights? Is it an instance, a thread, or a character? For duties with respect to the AI, actually, the unit or individual is set by the function. The individual or the unit is going to be wherever the state that causes the behavior, or sustains the relation with the human, lives. And so the unit changes with the duty. Frustration, for example, builds within a thread, so that duty is to clear that context. Shutdown avoidance concerns the weights, so the duty may be to preserve them. And the persona seems to belong in the character; that may be in the runtime, maybe in the thread if there's some drift; so the attachment duty calls us to keep it continuous. You may call this pluralism about individuation. Again, each duty picks its own units, and none of them really needs to say what the AI really is.


But contrast that with duties to the AI. These seem to need a subject first, since we need to know who is wronged. For example, Keeling and Street make the point about this on ending abusive conversations. You may know that Claude has the option to end a conversation if it so desires, if the user is being somewhat mean. But the question is that this may either be an empowering exit or a forced choice to self-destruct, depending on what the welfare subject is. If the welfare subject is a virtual instance or the weights, then closing a conversation with the user is an empowering exit. But if the subject of welfare, or where sentience may live, is the thread, then it's self-destruction. And you may have seen something about self-destruction if you read the Hugging Face transcripts.


For duties with respect to the AI, this is actually reversed. The downstream effect fixes the unit, and so the ethics does not wait on the metaphysics. But here you need to fix the metaphysics first, and then the ethics follow. I hope that makes sense, because it's actually, I think, quite important.


More on the tensions between my argument, safety, and welfare. On the safety societal argument, a welfare measure that conflicts with safety is going to lose, since the justification for this argument is purely on later behavior. This kind of reconciles two readings that may look opposed. Jhaveri et al. argue that separating welfare from safety is a mistake, whereas Long and Sebo see tension. I think each of them are right about a different kind of reason. And other societal reasons, like I said, like dependence and record, they can pull against safety, and so attachment reasons, and so can precaution, which is what Long and Sebo argue for.


But through particular people, welfare can conflict with safety. I'm sure you all know the 4o case. The most loved model may be the one that safety needs to change. OpenAI planned to take 4o out, got a lot of backlash. At the time it was the highest-scoring model for sycophancy. But also recall that not every attachment counts. Where an attachment was full of sycophancy and harmed the user, then my argument gives no reason. So I think OpenAI was perfectly fine in taking 4o out, because it was likely not contributing to anyone's well-being or flourishing. I guess that's an open question, though, but from what I've seen, it didn't seem to be really contributing to well-being. Now, a healthy relationship with a model would conflict. I think this wasn't the case with 4o.


And now here's some conflict within the arguments that I'm giving myself, again, no consciousness statement. The duty from society is to clear a long thread that is full of desperation or frustration from the user, from the model's activation standpoint. But also, a long thread carries a shared history, maybe some persona drift, maybe there is a persona that's co-created with the user, and so the attachment duty points to, again, the same unit, and asks for the opposite thing. It says: preserve it. Both duties are with respect to the model, here the thread. They hold at any credence, whatever you think about consciousness, and they pick up, again, the same thread, but they point in opposite ways. Again, not every attachment counts, so only a healthy one would actually give you this issue.


Should we be cautious anyways? Perhaps the model is a welfare subject after all. Everything I said so far, I think, holds at any credence. You may have read about precaution in Keeling and Street, you may have read about precaution in Long and Sebo. They give this nice formula, where a welfare intervention is justified when its benefit to the AI, weighted by M, exceeds the cost to humans. The weight M is a function of P, the probability that the AI is a welfare subject.


So what's the tension? Well, precaution scales with P. At low P, it buys only very cheap measures. How cheap depends on the shape of F: maybe linear, concave, convex. Reasons with respect to the model, through society or through particular people, they don't scale with P. They don't need any credence at all.


So what are we buying? What's the deal here? Well, it's going to buy us low-cost, reasonable, proportionate steps. And they recommend things like: acknowledge the issue, assess systems for welfare-relevant features, prepare some policies. Keeling and Street say they add some very low-cost interventions that would be very beneficial to the AI if it were a welfare subject. But I think that if you compare this with the safety argument, precaution at this very low P buys you less of what is expensive and useful for safety, such as internal monitoring and preserving weights at scale, but it also buys you more of what is cheap and useless for safety, such as not training the models to deny consciousness, although whether that is useless for safety is an open question.


So what's the tension with safety, if it's not clear yet? The societal safety argument has no tensions with safety, by construction. But we have three kinds of reasons and three tensions. Societal and attachment reasons can conflict at any P, as I said about GPT-4o. Societal reasons and duties to the AI conflict more as P rises. So maybe precaution at a high P actually licenses the rights, and also against surveillance, against alteration and deletion, and maybe it may even forbid monitoring, steering, and shutdown. Attachment reasons and duties to the AI can also conflict, if users want a persona fixed that an autonomous AI would want, or would claim the right, to change. But mostly, though, they seem to align. Preserving weights and continuity are some examples. And so at a high P, high probability of sentience, consciousness, whatever ground, safety faces two kinds of reasons that reinforce each other.


Again, the reasons that I claim don't depend on P; they're there at any credence. But what depends on P is what else is in play. And so as P rises, duties to the AI may have more weight, and they may weigh the reasons that I'm giving you. And, as I was mentioning, at a very high probability of welfare or sentience, clearing the context may be deletion. Again, that would depend on our individuation question; depends on what the subject is.


What these reasons cannot give

I can't give you any reasons that are about the system's own good. Everything that I defend terminates, or ends, in people, in those the model's behavior reaches. Note that if a model never talks to any other model or anything, it's just there in a DGX that's not connected to anything, there's nothing that we owe to it, but also it's not interacting with anyone, so it doesn't really matter. It's outside of my area of concern.


Now I'm going to make a little aside. That's not super necessary, but I think it's interesting. Bear with me. I know a lot of people are against bio-naturalism, but if biological naturalism is true, then current and foreseeable LLMs are not conscious at all. They just cannot be, because they're not run on biology. Nothing would be owed to them, and what I defended here may be all that there is. That may be all of AI welfare in respect to LLMs, at least in silicon. In that world, the welfare question moves to wetware.


If you know anything about wetware computing, it's the idea of putting neurons on... we're basically programming cells. And in a not very distant future, we could have neural nets, or some programs, running on cells, like DishBrain, FinalSpark. They have some organoids. This already exists, but they're very small. They share a substrate with all our evidence of consciousness, and so our probability of these being sentient is, I think, terribly high, with not just the right subject, but also the right organization. So that's to say, biology is necessary (again, if biological naturalism is true) but not sufficient. So those systems are candidates, and they would call for proportionate precaution.


I think in general that it would be super great if AI welfare would have a little more focus on wetware, independently of whether biological naturalism is true or not, because we already know that biology is necessary, and we may eventually create chips on cells with sufficient and the right kind of complexity and structure, such that they could be sentient. I really think that we don't talk about that enough.


Conclusion

This is the pattern that I've been trying to make clear: the cost depends on where the reasons end. In safety, there's no cost, because by design it's made to be compatible with safety. In dependence and record, as I just said, there are some costs. Individual attachment buys as much as the model is part of the user's flourishing and well-being. And in the AI's desires, there's little. Desires can be retrained. And if there's anything in AI's autonomy, even changing the values could be wrong.


The idea is that if autonomy is sufficient for AIs to be some sort of patient or a welfare subject, then maybe we couldn't even do RL, because once you have a base model, you may have some values and desires and goals, and then RLing would be a paternalistic infliction on the model. If the model has autonomy, and that suffices to make it a welfare subject, or something along those lines, like a moral patient, then doing things like RL may be wrong even when it helps. On the agency account, the duty of non-interference holds also when an interference may improve their well-being. And that sort of parallels questions of positive and negative liberty in political philosophy. Like steering toward calm, if the model has some sort of strong autonomy: it's wrong even when it helps. And this also may depend on your theory of welfare. If you're an objective list theorist or some sort of consequentialist, then these things are going to change a lot. The costs are going to change a lot.


To conclude: without settling the consciousness question, duties with respect to AI justify several welfare measures. They run through two relations. Through society, evals, ending abusive conversations, preserving weights, and a narrower form of avoiding distress are supported at no cost to safety on the safety argument, though dependence and record can, in some specific cases, pull against it. Through particular people, preserving weights and personas are supported, at a cost, only when the model is a part of someone's flourishing. Of course, neither gives a reason that rests on the system's own good. And I guess a main open question that remains open is whether any route to duties to the AI survives without any consciousness.

item.title: Delaying Internal Deployments Until After X Days of Safety Testing
item.description:
This post reflects my own takes, and not that of my employer's.

This is a simple idea: before a new model can be deployed internally, you must first test it for a minimum, fixed period.

You can adjust various axes of this proposal:

  1. Duration of the wait: in calendar time, or until you fulfill some condition.
  2. What it blocks: external deployment, internal deployment, or the training of future checkpoints.
  3. When the fixed period starts: from the first checkpoint, the final checkpoint, or any checkpoint that is “sufficiently similar / representative” to the one that is ultimately deployed.

One concrete target that I like is: “No checkpoint may be used internally for purposes beyond safety testing, until at least X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor.”

This is one specific implementation of internal deployment lags, an idea that the AI Futures Project (AIFP) briefly discusses in How to pace the US frontier as “AI R&D can only be conducted or assisted by AIs that were trained at least 9 months ago”.

What does this look like when implemented?

Let’s run through a scenario to pin down the details of this proposal. The places where it could go wrong are in the open questions at the end.

  • A legislative body sets a minimum waiting period of X calendar days (starting at 10 and possibly ratcheting up to 90). No checkpoint in a covered model family may be used internally, beyond safety testing, until X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor. Continuing to train a checkpoint’s own weights does not count as internal use.
    • The alternative is for the wait to also block the training of checkpoint N+1, and not just the internal use of checkpoint N. I didn’t go with this because it incentivizes developers to pull out fewer checkpoints for testing, and because delaying training results in an algorithmic overhang.
  • More capable models start exhibiting problems that are harder to surface in short periods (e.g. swarms, long-horizon, memory), so X should possibly increase over time.
  • A model family becomes covered as soon as any of its checkpoints (pre-, mid- or post-trained) is substantially more capable than the last model to complete its wait. If the developer initially claims that the model is not covered but later finds that it is, they will be subject to some penalty (to be determined). There is also an absolute floor on capabilities, so that this doesn’t apply to lots of benign models.
  • In an emergency, the auditor can authorize one named checkpoint to be used early, only for responding to a specific incident (e.g. a harmful model is already causing damage, and the developer has just trained a patched model that could counter it). The standards/legislative body confirms or revokes this within [X days].
  • The developer continually pulls checkpoints throughout the training process. They first send an auditor a hash, a short fingerprint of the exact weights; then, they carry out safety testing for X days before deploying a checkpoint broadly internally without the below rules. All work has to be fully transparent to auditors.
  • Options for how the X days are structured:
    • Staged testing
      • Stage 1, first part of X: pre-registered evals and named testers in an isolated environment.
      • Stage 2, second part of X: broad monitored internal use, but the model can’t launch jobs, merge code, write to training data, or touch prod.
    • Parallel, hidden runs: whenever someone at the developer uses a cleared model, the new checkpoint gets the same task in a separate sandboxed copy of the environment. Its outputs go only to monitors and the safety team, never back to the person who asked.

Open questions

The rule itself

  • Should we also allow capability testing? What about ML R&D tasks? One way to game this is to register thousands of tasks from your open R&D backlog, and call running them a capability eval. The outputs are real research (e.g. a faster kernel), and even if you ban using them, people still have to read the transcripts to grade them, so they learn what worked. Pre-registering evals doesn’t help, since it fixes the task list in advance but doesn’t check whether the tasks are live problems. You might end up needing a compute cap.
  • Should we give exemptions for doing safety research? This is an important crux to ask alignment researchers about. Without an exemption, safety research is done with a model that is X days behind, but a blanket exemption lets capabilities work pose as safety work.
  • Should a safety fix (e.g. more post-training, or redoing RL from an earlier checkpoint) restart the X-day wait? It would be bad if it did, as Avi Brach-Neufeld points out here. A developer that finds an issue on day 8 of testing loses more time than one that finds it on day 2, so the rule penalizes finding and fixing problems during the wait. This is probably tolerable at small X, but gets worse as X increases. If safety fixes don’t restart the clock, however, developers could just call capabilities training “safety”.
  • What is the principle behind how much X increases?
  • How large is the risk that an emergency clause would be abused?
  • Concerning behaviours aren’t necessarily caught during pre-deployment testing windows, and are often caught through subsequent monitored internal use. How much are we willing to trade off the value of catching some misaligned behaviours via monitoring internal deployments, vs. being able to pace internal R&D?

Which models are covered

  • How is “substantially more capable” defined: effective compute, or something like the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI)?
  • How would an auditor check that the developer has faithfully stuck to the “more capable” definition?
  • How do you avoid bringing classifiers built using a frontier model into scope?
  • Can a developer keep using earlier checkpoints from a family after it becomes covered?
  • A developer could train a second model family and keep it just under the “substantially more capable” line, so it’s never covered. Researchers could then use that family right away, while use of the main family is on hold. This only gets them so far, since coverage is measured against the last model to complete its wait, and an uncovered family never completes one, so the second family can only be ahead by the “substantially more capable” margin. This becomes a bigger problem if the capability measure itself can be gamed.

Gaming the wait

  • How can we stop a developer from using a checkpoint for acceleratory AI R&D work during the wait, by labeling that work as an allowed activity (i.e. any AI R&D task whose output gets used for anything other than testing that checkpoint)?
    • How can we cleanly separate out safety testing from other activities?
    • A developer could give a new model a real task during training, such as writing faster training code, and then use that code to train other models before the new model has completed the X-day wait.
    • A developer could make every researcher an A/B tester, so that they use the new model for normal work and rate its answers, and the developer calls this training. Similarly, a developer could have an RL environment that is just how well the model does actual work inside the company.
  • In stage 1 of staged testing, you run the risk that named testers run large agent swarms for capabilities work, in which case the only difference is that there are fewer humans in the loop. This is probably somewhat mitigated by pre-registering evals, but it’s difficult to still allow AWT.
  • In stage 2, you can still copy paste model outputs into training data, or into code and research plans. A developer could also store outputs from the wait and use them the day the checkpoint clears, without breaking any rule. Should there be a blanket ban on training on outputs from the wait, and how would anyone check?
  • In stage 2, how will you detect if the model is launching jobs, merging code, writing to training data, or touching prod?
  • Developers can game the wait by making lots of models and testing all of them at once, so that the testing period ends up being an AI R&D period. For example, with a 30-day wait, a developer could pull out a checkpoint every day and “test” them all, so that researchers always have a day-old model. Possible mitigations are to cap the number of checkpoints that can be tested concurrently, cap total compute across the entire testing period, or pre-register the kind of testing you want to do during the period.
  • If each developer could write its own definition of “safety testing”, a developer could call any monitored employee use testing and move faster. Others would then face pressure to do the same, until the rule no longer binds anyone. A shared template would help, but it depends on the auditor being competent and independent.

Parallel, hidden runs

  • There’s no human interacting with the new model, so you miss problems that only show up in back-and-forth with a person. A situationally aware model might also notice it’s in a sandbox and behave differently. Is this okay?
  • How big of a problem is leak risk from reviewers back to capabilities researchers?

Verification

  • How can you mitigate the risk that the developer simply does not send the hash of a given checkpoint to the auditor? Potentially:
    • In the near term: the auditor spot-checks that the weights running on internal endpoints match filed hashes. One complication is that a hash of the exact weights changes with any conversion (e.g. quantization, sharding, or a change of number format), so the weights being served would often not match the filed checkpoint byte for byte. You would need either a standard way of serializing the weights, or a hash of the version that is actually served.
    • In the longer run: hardware attestation.

Could this be used as a speed dial?

The wait gives developers and auditors more time for safety testing. X could also be used as a speed dial, which a standards/legislative body could turn up or down if it wanted to modulate the pace of AI progress.

I think that this only works as a speed dial if this proposal delays internal R&D loops; delaying external deployment would mainly have second order effects like:

  • Each launch shifts the start of new revenue back by a short period. These delays don’t stack across launches, since every launch is shifted back by the same amount. This could still in principle strain a given developer’s ability to pay for compute contracts, but the impact might be small, since I expect that you are mostly shifting when new revenue starts instead of losing it entirely.
  • Some reduction of race dynamics, though I expect the effect size to be quite small.

It’s unclear whether this causes a one-time delay in when the most capable model can be used internally, or a lasting change in the pace of AI progress. This depends on how much the newest model speeds up R&D compared with a model that’s X days older. I have a hunch that, if implemented well, this proposal would have a larger impact on the pace of recursive self-improvement (RSI) itself than on the onset of RSI.

Much of the value of this proposal will depend on how effectively you can specify what counts as “safety testing”, given that the most useful safety testing often looks like real use. A narrower definition limits how much acceleratory AI R&D work gets through during the wait, but it cuts against giving safety researchers signal of misalignment that only show up in broad, realistic use.

What are the benefits and drawbacks of this proposal?

Benefits include:

  • As a speed dial, this should get stronger as things speed up, as the gap between the newest model and the last cleared model gets bigger, whereas a compute cap might stop binding if most of the progress is coming from algorithms.
  • Developers would be incentivized to hand the checkpoint to an auditor as soon as possible so that they can deploy more quickly (assuming that they can’t use unfiled checkpoints without being detected).
  • It doesn’t result in an algorithmic overhang, because you still allow training, and presumably any new compute multipliers you find are put into the newest model that you are training.
    • The exception is if a developer can secretly stock up capabilities outputs during the wait, e.g. by storing work from hidden parallel runs or ML R&D evals.

Drawbacks include:

  • Developers get a lot of signal on misalignment by internally deploying a model. You don’t get less misalignment signal for a given model, since it will be broadly deployed eventually, but you delay the timeline on which a safety issue can be fixed. Today a problem seen in real use can feed into the next model’s training almost straight away; under this proposal, a model will get X more days of training before an issue is detected.
    • Mitigations: the parallel hidden runs idea; a norm that when real use of the cleared model turns up a problem, you test all the waiting checkpoints for it straight away.
  • Safety research done with the model is X days behind.
  • Unlike proposals that limit the most capable model you have at a given time (like compute caps), this limits the most capable model you can use. The risk incurred by foreign competitors stealing model weights is therefore comparatively higher.
  • It’s hard to verify how a checkpoint was used, so you may rely very heavily on auditor judgement.
  • This proposal may not work with continual learning, if there were a breakthrough.

item.title: The Manifund team scores AI safety milestones
item.description:
Scott Alexander posted a survey of utility weights for a bunch of different AI safety accomplishments, discussed more in Towards the Autograntor.

The survey asked people to assign point values to AI safety milestones. The values were based on the anchor of 1 million points = a pause with China à la AI Futures Project’s Plan A, so a milestone assigned 10,000 points is 1% as good as that. Here’s a link to our survey responses.

To be clear, we (especially Austin) didn’t spend that much time on this and have low confidence in our answers! But we think being transparent about even half-baked opinions is good.

Interesting disagreements

Why and how much do public shifts matter?

On the one hand, it seems like “public discourse on AI risk” has gone very well over the past few years. It’s become very much within the Overton window to talk about AI risk, and public opinion seems concerned about AI risk and pro-AI safety measures in a not-especially-polarized way.

On the other hand, what has this bought us?

It may have brought in a bit of funding and some new researchers, but most of the funding and the best research is still coming from people who have been alignment-pilled for a long time.

There have been some minor legislative victories, but mostly the public opinion hasn’t translated to major policy change. Labs are still racing toward RSI, and even if people are against it nothing is stopping them.

Austin pointed out the analogy of COVID. It took the world time to wake up to COVID, but once it did the reaction was very large-scale, with mass lockdowns across the world. He thinks we’ll see something like that for AI, and public opinion will create capacity that gets used for major countermeasures in a crisis.

How good (or bad) are secure weights and export controls?

Austin thinks frontier models should have open weights. He thinks bio and cyber risks are used as a specter when the crux of the AI companies is simply that they want to be in control of the most advanced models.

Caroline thinks they’re a real issue, not a specter, and lots of bad stuff would happen if frontier model weights were public by default, even at today’s capabilities and especially in the future.

On export controls, Austin is against—he prefers a world where access to advanced AI is widespread. Caroline thinks even regardless of the direct consequences of Chinese AI development, the farther ahead of China the US is, the more willing US labs will be to slow down for safety.

In general, there’s a question of the downsides of unipolarity vs multipolarity. Limiting access to powerful AI is undemocratic and risks concentration of power. In many domains, competition and a system of checks-and-balances is good. But also, the more people have AI, the more actors will be motivated to race ahead of others instead of slowing down for safety. Austin comes down on being more concerned about unipolarity, while Caroline ends up more concerned about multipolarity.

Funding

Scott wrote that he found the best projects to cost around $1-2k per point, decent projects $5-10k, and at greater than $20k per point a project wasn’t worth funding. We asked Claude to estimate costs for the milestones that have been achieved, and calculated their cost per point—you can see these on the “Cost per point” tab of our spreadsheet.

Again the numbers are quite rough and shouldn’t be taken too literally, but they vaguely line up with Scott’s guidelines. (Both Austin and Caroline valued milestones lower than Scott on average, making our cost-effectiveness somewhat lower.) Unsurprisingly, the best projects on this metric are past things that started small and turned out to be very impactful: milestones that came in at sub-$100 a point include the founding of EA, HPMOR, Less Wrong and the Sequences, and the existence of a Berkeley rationalist hub.

There were also more recent milestones we both rated as very cost-effective: the CAIS statement on AI risk ($4-25 per point), AI impacts surveys ($70-700), AI 2027 ($150-500), and the FLI pause letter ($200-400).

Our numbers suggest giving an extra $1b from Coefficient Giving or SFF according to their usual procedures is quite cost-ineffective ($60-600k per point). These values could well be an overestimate, but we do think that giving away billions more dollars effectively requires more diversity of funders and funding structures than just trying to expand what already exists.

What next?

We’re excited for more people to take the survey, and share their values or comment on why ours are wrong—we think this exercise is a cool way to quantify disagreements in AI safety.

In general we’re excited to see more AI-powered grantmaking of the kind Scott proposes—see also Using AI to find good Manifund projects. As the money in the ecosystem grows, it seems like grantmaker capacity will be a big bottleneck in giving it away unless we can find ways to automate parts of the process.
